title: Fewest Slides to Solve a Six-Tile Board
statement:
A small sliding puzzle has 2 rows and 3 columns. Five tiles numbered 1 to 5 sit on it, and the remaining cell is the gap, written as 0.

One move slides a tile that is directly above, below, left or right of the gap into the gap. The puzzle is solved when the board reads [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 0]].

Given the starting board, return the fewest moves needed to solve it, or -1 if it cannot be solved.

examples.why: Slide the 4 left, then the 5 left. The gap ends up in the bottom-right corner.
Only the 1 and 2 are swapped. Every move changes the arrangement by one swap with the gap, and a lone swap of two tiles can never be undone that way.
Slide 3, 2, 1, 4, 5 into the gap in that order: the gap travels left along the top row, down, then right along the bottom row.

constraints: board contains each of 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 exactly once
gen: (r, big) => { const p = r.shuffle([0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]); return [[p.slice(0, 3), p.slice(3)]]; }
hints: How many different boards are there in total? Small enough to explore all of them?
Each board is a node in a graph; a move is an edge to another board. The fewest moves is the shortest path in an unweighted graph.
Encode a board as a 6-character string, precompute which cells are next to each cell, and run BFS from the start until you reach "123450". If BFS runs out, return -1.

explain.intuition:
Instead of thinking about tiles, think about whole boards. There are only 6! = 720 of them. Each move turns one board into another, so the boards form a graph where every edge costs one move. The fewest moves is the shortest path from the starting board to the solved one, and in an unweighted graph BFS finds it: it reaches every board at distance 1, then distance 2, and so on.

The search space is tiny, so the work is in the bookkeeping. Flatten the board into a string like "123045", so it can go in a visited set. The gap moves within the flattened string to fixed neighbours: index 0 touches 1 and 3, index 1 touches 0, 2 and 4, and so on. Exactly half of the 720 boards can reach the goal. If BFS empties its queue without reaching it, the answer is -1.
steps: Flatten the board to a string; if it is already "123450", return 0.
BFS level by level from the start, marking boards as seen when they are queued.
For each board, find the gap, swap it with each neighbouring cell, and queue every unseen result. Return the level when the goal appears.
pitfalls: Using DFS. It finds a solution, not the shortest, and without a depth limit it can wander through all 360 reachable boards.
Computing neighbours with index ± 1 on the flat string. Index 2 and index 3 are not neighbours: they are the end of row 0 and the start of row 1.
Marking boards as seen only when they are dequeued. Then the same board is queued many times.

solutions.title: BFS over board states
solutions.idea: Every board is a node and every slide is an edge. Breadth-first search from the start gives the fewest moves.

solutions.title: Parity check, then BFS backwards from the goal
solutions.idea: Count inversions among the tiles: on a 3-wide board a move never changes their parity, so an odd count means -1 at once. Otherwise one BFS from the goal labels every reachable board with its distance.

followups: Scale up to the 4 × 4 fifteen-puzzle. Why does plain BFS break down, and how do A* with a Manhattan-distance heuristic or bidirectional BFS help?
Return the actual sequence of moves, not just how many.
